summary.text: 饿 means “hungry.” It is the simplified form of 餓, whose traditional construction pairs 食, the food-related element, with 我 as a sound component.

formation.text: The traditional character 餓 is phonosemantic: 食 supplies the food-related meaning and 我 supplies a sound cue. In simplified 饿, 食 is written in its conventional left-side form 饣; this is a graphic standardization of the character, not a separate ancient construction.

components.text: 饣 is the simplified left-side form corresponding to 食 in traditional 餓. 食 marks the food-related category; the difference between these forms reflects simplification, not a historical sequence.
我 is the phonetic component in 餓. The Zhengzhang comparison supports this role, although the reconstructed forms differ in their endings; Mandarin readings wǒ and è are not identical today.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang Old Chinese, 我 *ŋaːlʔ and 餓 *ŋaːls share a segmental base but differ in ending. These are system-specific reconstructions, not recorded pronunciations.

history.text: The traditional graph is described with 食 on the left and 我 on the right. Reference lists report a Qin-slip specimen and a transmitted ancient form, but these do not establish a detailed sequence of graphic changes.
The simplified form 饿 represents 食 with its simplified left-side form 饣. This is a character-to-character standardization, not evidence that 饣 came before 食.

uncertainties.text: The precise early graphic sequence and earliest attestation remain unresolved. The reported Qin-slip form has not been visually verified, and no secure oracle-bone or bronze form is established by these references.
The original object represented by 我 is disputed, and its proposed original name and pronunciation remain unresolved. This does not undermine the independently supported phonetic role of 我 in 餓.

senses.text: The traditional character 餓 is glossed as 飢, “hungry,” and literary citations show its use for being hungry. These are the earliest supported sense and attestations here, though their dates do not establish when the character was first used.

senses.period: some early literary usage; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: Some reported early passages distinguish 餓 from 飢 by degree, using 餓 for more severe hunger. This limited contrast is not a complete account of their historical meanings.

senses.gloss: make hungry; cause to suffer hunger
senses.text: A literary citation records a causative use meaning “make hungry.” Its timing relative to the intransitive sense “be hungry” is unresolved.

senses.gloss: poor; lacking, including lack of water
senses.period: later dialectal usage; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: Later dialect examples use the word for being poor or lacking, including fields short of water. The evidence does not show when this sense arose or how it developed from “hungry.”
“Greedy for” appears among modern glosses, but its chronology and relationship to “hungry” are unresolved.

developments.text: Some reported early usage uses 餓 for more severe hunger than 飢. This is a limited distinction in usage, not a full account of historical meaning.

limitations.text: The literary and manuscript citations do not provide dates sufficient to establish the first attestation or a full chronology of the senses.
The evidence does not establish how “hungry” developed into “poor” or “lacking,” or when that sense arose.
The modern gloss “greedy for” has no dated or otherwise supported semantic history here.

relationships.text: In 饿, 饣 is the simplified positional form corresponding to 食, which provides the food-related semantic category.
饿 is the simplified form of 餓; 食 is represented by its simplified positional form 饣.
In 餓, 我 supplies a sound cue, supported by the same-system Zhengzhang Old Chinese comparison.

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry for 餓 quotes the Shuowen definition “飢也。从食，我聲” and gives modern Mandarin è. It cites the Analects (伯夷叔齊，餓于首陽之下) for the intransitive hunger sense, the Book of Rites for hungry people, and the Mencius (餓其體膚) for a causative ‘make hungry’ use. The entry documents those classical citations but does not provide their composition dates; they establish literary attestations, not the character’s first-ever use.
evidence.title: [A04598] 餓 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.field: 說文解字; 音韻方言; 字源字形
evidence.text: 漢典 reproduces the Shuowen statement ‘飢也。从食我聲。五箇切’; it reports Standard Mandarin è, Cantonese ngo6, and the Tang-period reading ngɑ̀. It lists Middle Chinese 疑母, 箇韻, 去聲, 五个切, and labels the old readings as Huang Kan and Wang Li systems, 疑母歌部. Its graphic sequence lists Shuowen small seal, Qin-system slips, clerical, and regular script; it identifies a Qin slip specimen as 睡.日甲62背. This is a reported chart/specimen inventory, not an inspected glyph image.
evidence.title: 餓 è - 汉典

evidence.text: The dictionary groups early citations under hunger and causative hunger. It cites the Huainanzi, ‘無一月餓’, and Han Feizi, ‘家有常業，雖飢不餓’, as evidence that some early usage distinguished 餓 from 飢 by degree; it also cites the Analects for 伯夷、叔齊餓於首陽之下 and Mencius for 餓其體膚. It reports a later extension ‘poor; lacking’ with dialect examples such as water-starved fields. These are dictionary-reported attestations and senses; the page does not independently date the quoted works or establish a precise semantic path from hunger to lack.
evidence.title: 餓 è - 汉典

evidence.text: The separate graph-history page displays a transmitted ancient form labelled 海4.37 and supplies bibliography references to 睡虎地秦簡文字編 (p./line 76.6), 秦簡牘文字編 (p.147), and 傳抄古文字編. Its visible category list includes Qin-system slips and Shuowen small seal. The page itself does not explain the glyph’s component interpretation or give an oracle-bone or bronze form.

evidence.text: The 餓 entry identifies 我 as its sound-series element and gives 餓 Zhengzhang Old Chinese *ŋaːls. The opened 我 entry lists 我 *ŋaːlʔ in the same Zhengzhang system and 餓 *ŋaːls among its series members. This same-system comparison supports the phonetic relation despite tone/coda differences. evidence.text: The database’s 我 page lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and small-seal categories, and asserts that the original graph depicted an ancient weapon described as a long-handled axe-like object with toothed edge; it says the graph was later borrowed for the first-person pronoun and the weapon sense fell out of use. The borrowed pronoun’s history does not independently prove the weapon’s original name or pronunciation. That name remains unrecovered in the evidence inspected here, so this account cannot be used to establish an additional whole-graph borrowing sound match.

evidence.text: The entry presents the weapon-identification as a pictographic proposal and notes Jao and Zeng’s conjecture about a three-bladed polearm, while recording Guo Moruo’s alternative identification with 錡, a toothed battle axe. It separately records a folk etymology analyzing a hand holding a weapon. Thus the exact depicted object is disputed; the phonetic use of 我 within 餓 does not depend on choosing among those object identifications.

evidence.source: 中央研究院 / 漢典 reference synthesis
evidence.text: The most economical supported analysis is traditional 餓 = semantic 食 plus phonetic 我, following the Shuowen account and consistent with the Zhengzhang same-system comparison. 饣 is a modern simplified positional form of 食 in the simplified character 饿, not an independently established ancient component of 餓. No evidence located in this research supports an ideographic or mnemonic analysis for 餓.
evidence.title: [A04598] 餓 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: Standard Mandarin 餓 is è and 我 is wǒ; the entries also report Cantonese 餓 ngo6 and 我 ngo5 (Jyutping), and Tang-period 餓 ngɑ̀ and 我 *ngɑ̌ (漢典). The Zhengzhang Old Chinese comparison is 餓 *ŋaːls versus 我 *ŋaːlʔ. These do not match exactly in tone/coda but share the segmental base in that reconstruction; phonetic components need not have identical modern readings. Variation and transcription systems differ across these records.

These do not match exactly in tone/coda but share the segmental base in that reconstruction; phonetic components need not have identical modern readings. Variation and transcription systems differ across these records.
evidence.title: 餓 è - 汉典

evidence.text: The entry identifies 饿 as the simplified form of 餓, with 食 replaced by its simplified left-side form 饣; this is a graphic standardization relationship, not a historical ancestor relationship between distinct forms.

evidence.text: The entry quotes the Shuowen analysis 飢也。从食，我聲 and gives the pronunciation è. It cites the Analects for the intransitive ‘be hungry’ use and the Mencius for the causative ‘make hungry’ use. These are citations to literary works, not dates for the character’s first use.
evidence.title: [A04598] 餓 - Ministry of Education 《Dictionary of Chinese Character Varients》2024

evidence.text: The entry reports the Analects and Mencius examples and cites the Huainanzi and Han Feizi in support of a distinction in some early usage between 飢 (less severe hunger) and 餓 (more severe hunger). It also lists later dialectal uses for ‘poor; lacking’, but does not establish when that sense arose or its path from hunger.

evidence.text: The page describes 餓 as 从食、我聲 and cites the Analects, Zhuangzi, Han Feizi and a Mawangdui silk manuscript of the Zhouyi. The page calls the Mawangdui item ‘第9行’ and quotes a phrase with 飢餓不得食. The source gives no dating details for that manuscript citation on this entry.

evidence.text: The page reports one 餓 occurrence in the Qin Shuihudi slips, identified as 睡‧日甲62背, and says its written form may use 飢 with 我 as phonetic; it describes the seal form as regularized to 食 plus 我. It labels the character first attested in Warring States script. This is a secondary report, not an inspected artifact image or an independently verified reading.

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) and Baxter–Sagart (2014)
evidence.text: The entry identifies 我 as the phonetic component of 餓 and lists 餓 as Zhengzhang Old Chinese *ŋaːls and 我 as *ŋaːlʔ, a same-system comparison supporting the sound relationship despite differing endings. It also lists Baxter–Sagart 餓 *ŋˤaj-s. The component’s modern readings differ: 餓 è in Standard Mandarin and ngo6 in Jyutping Cantonese; 我 wǒ in Standard Mandarin and ngo5 in Jyutping Cantonese. Reconstructions are system-specific proposals, not directly recorded speech.

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) and Baxter–Sagart (2014)
evidence.text: The 我 entry lists Zhengzhang *ŋaːlʔ and Baxter–Sagart *ŋˤajʔ, supporting comparison with 餓 within each reconstruction system. Its account of the earliest graphic referent is disputed: it describes weapon or tool interpretations and an alternative identification with 錡, while noting a folk analysis. Even if the first-person pronoun is analyzed as a phonetic loan of the graph, that does not independently recover the weapon’s name or pronunciation. This uncertainty does not negate 我’s later phonetic role in 餓.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No primary inscription image for 餓 was visually inspected. Although Han Dian lists a Qin-system slip specimen as 睡.日甲62背 and a transmitted ancient form 海4.37, the exact forms and scholarly readings remain unverified here.
No secure oracle-bone or bronze attestation for 餓 was established. The absence of such evidence in inspected pages is not proof that no form exists.

The Sinica 餓 evolution link failed (cache miss), and the Ytenx page plus Guoxuedashi graph-history page failed to open. These access failures limit verification of detailed graphic stages and phonological database records.

The proposed original object depicted by 我 is disputed among weapon identifications. Its original spoken name/pronunciation was not recovered; the first-person pronoun’s reconstruction alone cannot establish that object name. This uncertainty does not undermine the independently reported 我 sound-series role in 餓.

No independently sourced Qin-Han dated citation beyond the sources’ citations to classical works was inspected. The MOE page provides textual citations but not composition dates or manuscript witnesses, so exact earliest attestation chronology remains unresolved.
The extension from hunger to poverty/lack is attested in dictionary examples but its historical semantic bridge and chronology are not established by the inspected evidence.
The consulted evidence does not substantiate corruption in 餓. Shuowen’s component interpretation is a historical source assertion, not a directly inspected early glyph confirmation.

The Zhengzhang forms were available for both 餓 and 我. Baxter–Sagart was reported for 餓, but an inspected corresponding 我 form was not established in this research, so comparison in that system is incomplete.
For simplified 饿, the relationship is described as 食 to 饣; there is no basis here for assigning an earlier-form origin relation to 饣.
No direct pixel inspection was performed. No 餓/饿 image with confirmed character identity and reuse rights was established, so the historical glyph image list is empty.

The Guoxuedashi page was surfaced by search but its direct opening failed. Its claim of a Qin slip form that may be written with 飢 plus phonetic 我 is retained only as a reported secondary analysis, not verified paleographic fact.
No secure oracle-bone or bronze attestation was established. Han Dian and the reported Qin-slip source inventory begin with later material; this does not prove earlier forms do not exist.

The Qin slip is identified as 睡.日甲62背. A separate accessible Sinica source describes its Qin slips database as based on traced and digitized forms from a published character compilation; no exact 餓 image was available through this research, so image-based form comparison is unresolved.
The earliest semantic attestation remains undated here. The sources cite classical works and a Mawangdui manuscript but do not give exact composition or manuscript dates tied to each 餓 quotation.

A degree contrast between 飢 and 餓 is reported for some early literary usage, but it should not be generalized as the only ancient meaning distinction. Later ‘poor/lacking’ examples are recorded without a proven semantic bridge or chronology.

The weapon/tool interpretation for the graph 我 is disputed and its proposed original name/pronunciation has not been independently recovered. That unresolved whole-graph loan question does not undermine the independently supported use of 我 as a phonetic component in 餓.
No evidence inspected supports graphic corruption in 餓. Shuowen’s analysis is an ancient lexicographic assertion, while the reported Qin graph is not visually verified.
The source’s Proto-Sino-Tibetan cognate proposal for the spoken hunger word is separate from 餓’s graphic formation and was not independently assessed in this research.

limitations.text: No supplied glyph image could be verified as a legible image of 餓 or 饿, so none is selected. The listed Qin slip and transmitted form are reported in reference sources, but their pixels were not available for inspection.
